urls.description: This dataset provides annual updates of eleven headline indicators of the state of the climate system and of the human influence on it. The indicators combine several origins: emission inventories, in situ and satellite observations (such as surface temperature, ocean heat content, sea level and sea surface temperature records), the ERA5 reanalysis, and established statistical and model-based methods used to estimate radiative forcing, to attribute the observed warming to human activity and to derive the remaining carbon budget. The indicators follow the chain from cause to effect: greenhouse gas emissions, atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations, effective radiative forcing, the Earth energy imbalance, observed global temperature, human-induced warming (temperature attribution), the remaining carbon budget (CO2 budget), and a set of climatic impact-drivers comprising sea level rise, marine heatwaves, land temperature extremes and land precipitation. Investigators point to a Japanese-invested telecom firm #Mobicom convoy that drove into the no-entry zone during peak fire season -- dry grass under one vehicle ignited and strong winds did the rest. 🚗💨

Mongolia rushed 606 firefighters; China deployed 3,400 along the border. 🚨⚖

#ClimateChange has already pushed Mongolia's temperatures up 2.5°C since 1941 and left 82% of its land degraded, making steppes far more flammable -- nearly 80% of fires are human-caused. 🌡🌍 https://t.co/hnitM3D5l2

Ukrainian drones took out three data centers owned by Yandex, the internet conglomerate sometimes referred to as Russia’s Google, last week in retaliation for Russian strikes on its data centers.

The strikes caused severe disruptions across the country, impeding Russians’ ability to send emails, make payments, and navigate the streets.

"These strikes will have minimal effect on the global race to develop and adopt artificial intelligence," writes expert @ConnorMauthor. "Russia is nowhere close to the cutting edge of the field . . . hamstrung by lack of access to cutting-edge chips and by a brain drain of engineers."

“But the bigger implication of the Ukrainian strikes is that they have laid bare a fundamental risk to the development and deployment of AI worldwide: its physical infrastructure is vulnerable.”

“Companies and nations seeking to protect their data centers should therefore pursue a strategy of redundancy and resiliency.”

“At its highest levels of performance, AI’s capabilities can appear otherworldly—but it is fundamentally a technology dependent on physical things. Defending it is just a new version of the oldest problem in warfare: how to hit your enemy’s infrastructure while stopping them from hitting yours.”

"As long as they provide value, data centers will be targets," Martin writes. "Countries and companies are well advised to prepare for that future now.”
